interactions.summary: A student reads the transition into the next sphere of Paradise, including Beatrice's line telling Dante to trust the souls as he trusts God and the approach of the spirit who will identify himself in the next canto.

Jiang identifies the speaker as Justinian, then asks the class to notice the shocking word in Beatrice's instruction and uses it to highlight a sacrilegious-sounding plurality within a Christian heaven.

A student asks whether the word points back to Greek gods and Dante's earlier invocations of Apollo and the Muses, and Jiang agrees, using that opening to argue that the Divine Comedy quietly subverts orthodox Christian reading habits.

claims.claim: The read-aloud passage has Beatrice telling Dante to trust the approaching soul as he trusts God, even though the scene is set within the triumphant order of heaven.
Jiang identifies the newly encountered spirit as Justinian, the Byzantine emperor who will narrate Roman and church history in the next canto.
Jiang says the disturbing word in the passage is 'God' because within Christian monotheism it becomes sacrilegious to speak as if there were subordinate gods in heaven.
A student suggests the line may refer back to Greek gods because Dante earlier invoked Apollo and the Muses while still writing as a Christian poet.
Jiang accepts the pagan reference and says the point is to introduce a subordinate-god possibility that destabilizes a purely monotheistic reading.
Jiang says most readers treat the Divine Comedy as a straightforward Christian text, but small embedded details throughout the poem subvert traditional Christianity if one reads deeply enough.
Jiang says the next canto will present the official Catholic chronology from Rome to the Holy Roman Empire even as the poem contains small details that work against that official frame.
claims.temporal_scope: Forecast and interpretive frame stated on 2026-06-18.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang isolates the word 'God' as the line's scandal, forcing the class to hear how strange it is for heaven to speak as if trust could be distributed below the one God.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's key interpretive crack: Dante's heaven suddenly sounds less doctrinally sealed than orthodox Christianity would permit.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang argues that the Divine Comedy contains tiny embedded subversions that overturn a merely official Christian reading if the reader attends to them closely.
signature_moments.source_phrase: small things embedded throughout the text that subvert
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It captures Jiang's method of reading Dante against doctrinal surface while staying inside the poem's Catholic architecture.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's provocative label for the implication that Dante's heaven may contain beings addressed with a trust relation that sounds too close to divinity for strict monotheism.
Jiang's phrase for the small embedded details in Dante that destabilize a purely orthodox Christian reading without abandoning the Christian framework.

chronology_notes.note: On 2026-06-18 Jiang frames Justinian's canto as both official church chronology and covert doctrinal disturbance, emphasizing that Dante's Christian cosmos carries pagan or polytheistic residue inside it.
